common_name: Purple Robe Mossy Saxifrage (Carmine-Red Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil; 'Purple Robe' forms a dense evergreen mat of tiny needle-like rosettes that resents standing winter wet more than it minds cold.

directions: Purple Robe is one of the long-cultivated Georg Arends hybrid mossy saxifrages, bred in Germany beginning in the late 1800s from crosses among European alpine Saxifraga species. It forms a tight, moss-like carpet of small dark-green rosettes that all but disappears under a flush of carmine-red, yellow-centered flowers on short stems in mid-spring. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates, where deep shade from taller shade perennials or a north-facing rock garden keeps the mat from browning out in summer heat. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage a tidier second flush of growth.

common_name: Peter Pan Mossy Saxifrage (Dwarf Carmine-Red Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the tight evergreen rosettes of 'Peter Pan' are even more compact than the species type and suit rock gardens, troughs, or shaded path edging.

directions: Peter Pan is a true dwarf among the Georg Arends mossy saxifrage hybrids, forming an especially tight, dark evergreen mat of needle-fine rosettes only a few inches tall. In mid-spring the foliage is almost obscured by a profusion of carmine-red, yellow-eyed flowers held on very short stems, making it a favorite for shaded rock gardens, stone wall crevices, and trough plantings where a larger mossy saxifrage would sprawl. Give it cool, evenly moist, sharply drained soil and shade from hot afternoon sun, which is what browns out mossy saxifrages more often than cold does. Divide congested mats every few years in early fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Cloth of Gold Saxifrage (Golden-Foliage Mossy Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil; grown primarily for its chartreuse-gold evergreen foliage, which colors best with a few hours of morning sun and shade for the rest of the day.

directions: Cloth of Gold is grown less for its small white spring flowers than for its foliage, a dense evergreen mat of finely divided golden-chartreuse leaves that brightens shaded rock gardens and path edges year-round. Like other mossy saxifrage hybrids bred from Georg Arends's late-19th-century crosses, it needs cool roots, sharp drainage, and protection from hot midday sun, which scorches the bright foliage color. It combines well planted among shade perennials such as Heuchera or Tiarella, where its low gold mat contrasts against darker foliage. Shear back hard after flowering if the mat becomes patchy to encourage fresh growth.

common_name: Touran White Mossy Saxifrage (Compact White-Flowered Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring into gritty, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Touran series was bred for uniform, heavy flowering and reliable performance in containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Touran White is a modern seed-propagated selection from the Touran series of mossy saxifrage, bred for compact, uniform mounds and an unusually long, heavy bloom period compared with older mossy saxifrage cultivars. Pure white, yellow-centered flowers cover the dense evergreen foliage mat in mid-spring, brightening shaded rock gardens, woodland edges, and mixed containers. Like other Arends-type mossy saxifrages it wants cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil and shade from hot afternoon sun, which browns the fine foliage. The tight, uniform habit of the Touran series makes it a reliable choice for mass planting under high shade where older seed strains bloomed less evenly.

common_name: Lime Rickey Smooth Hydrangea (Compact Jade-Green Wild Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil; 'Lime Rickey' blooms on new wood, so an annual late-winter cutback to a low framework encourages the strongest stems and largest mophead blooms.

directions: Lime Rickey is a Proven Winners introduction (patented as 'Dardom') of the North American native smooth hydrangea, selected for a compact habit and exceptionally sturdy stems that hold its large mophead blooms upright even in summer storms, unlike the floppier classic 'Annabelle'. Flower heads open a fresh lime green with a dusting of pink pollen, gradually age to jade and pearly white, and dry well for cutting. It flowers reliably on new wood from midsummer into fall even after a hard late-winter pruning, making it forgiving for gardeners who forget to prune on schedule. Give it a partly shaded site with consistently moist, fertile soil, since smooth hydrangea wilts quickly in dry spells despite its overall toughness.

common_name: Silver Wings Solomon's Seal (Twisted Gray-Backed Fragrant Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall into humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in partial to full shade; the arching stems of 'Silver Wings' hold their twisted leaf pairs at a distinctly upright angle compared with typical Solomon's seal.

directions: Silver Wings is a distinctive dwarf selection of fragrant Solomon's seal, notable for leaf pairs that twist and angle sharply upward along the arching stem rather than lying flat, exposing the grayish-green undersides of the foliage and the hanging rows of small green-tipped white flowers beneath. Like the species, it spreads slowly by rhizome to form an attractive woodland colony and carries small blue-black berries in fall after the spring flowers fade. It performs best in cool, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture in a shaded border or woodland garden, where its unusual upright leaf posture sets it apart from the many flatter-leaved Solomon's seal cultivars already common in cultivation.

common_name: Chinese Dragon Ligularia (Bold Cutleaf Sichuan Ligularia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; site out of drying wind and midday sun, since the large cutleaf foliage wilts dramatically in heat and dry soil even though plants usually recover by evening.

directions: Chinese Dragon was introduced by Plant Delights Nursery/Juniper Level Botanic Garden in 2011 from seed collected in Sichuan, China in 2005, and is classified with Ligularia japonica though its bold, deeply cut foliage is less finely serrated than the typical Japanese form of the species. Sturdy four-foot spikes of yellow-orange daisy flowers rise above the dramatic foliage clumps in early to midsummer, drawing pollinators to the shade border. Give it a moist to boggy site such as a pond or stream margin, since it shares the classic ligularia trait of wilting hard in any afternoon sun or soil dryness. Its large leaf texture makes a strong architectural contrast against ferns and finer-textured shade perennials.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden catalog

common_name: Silver Dollar Panicle Hydrangea (Compact Dutch-Bred Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall into well-drained, humus-rich soil; prune hard in late winter to a low framework since 'Silver Dollar' blooms on new wood and responds well to renewal pruning for larger panicles.

directions: Silver Dollar is a compact panicle hydrangea introduced around 1990 by Dutch plantsman Peter Zwijnenburg and awarded the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit in 2008. Dense conical flower panicles open pure white in midsummer and slowly take on a soft pink flush as they age into fall, holding well on sturdy stems without the floppiness of older paniculata seedlings. Its naturally rounded, symmetrical five-by-five-foot habit needs less corrective pruning than many panicle hydrangeas to keep a tidy shape. It tolerates part shade better than most sun-loving shrubs and adapts to a wide range of soils as long as drainage is adequate, making it a dependable mid-size choice for a woodland edge or foundation planting.

common_name: Skyfall Panicle Hydrangea (Recurved Hyacinth-Flowered Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall into well-drained, humus-rich soil; prune in late winter to a strong framework, since Skyfall blooms on new wood and its heavy flower clusters benefit from sturdy stem structure.

directions: Skyfall (patented as 'GRHPAST05', US Plant Patent 32,971) is distinguished among panicle hydrangeas by unusually large, dense flower clusters made up of individual florets with distinctly recurved petals, giving each cluster a hyacinth-like texture rather than the typical flat-petaled panicle look. Flowers open white in summer and age gradually to soft pale pink through fall, held on strong, upright stems. It tolerates full sun in cooler climates but appreciates part shade and consistent moisture in hotter regions, where afternoon shade helps flower color last longer without fading or browning. Its larger mature size compared with many modern panicle hydrangeas suits it to a background shrub border or as a specimen where its dramatic flower texture can be seen up close.

common_name: Pink Whisper Heucherella (Silvered Green Foamy Bells with Spring Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; also sold under the synonym 'Pink Gem'.

directions: Pink Whisper is a Terra Nova Nurseries foamy bells selection with green foliage brushed silver and traced with fine red venation, closely related in coloring to the earlier 'Kimono' but distinguished by a heavier flush of small pink flowers held on wiry stems well above the foliage in mid-spring. Like other Heucherella hybrids between Heuchera and Tiarella, it forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump that tolerates more shade and damp soil than most Heuchera while keeping better-defined leaf shape than most Tiarella. It looks best in bright, indirect shade with consistent moisture and light winter mulch in colder zones, and mixes well with hostas and ferns as a season-long foliage accent that adds a spring bloom bonus.
